Requirement 03.01.02 — Transaction & Function Control
Limit system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute.
03.01.02.a: The types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute are defined

Assessment objectives (a coverage checklist — do NOT copy their wording):
- the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute are defined

Evidence excerpts:
--- [Pellucid_Access_Control_Standard_v2.3.docx] (excerpt)
4.2 Permitted Functions by Role
Each Okta group maps to a defined set of permitted actions. Anything not listed is denied by default.
- PA-Engineering: read/write on assigned client GitHub repos, deploy to staging only, view Graylog streams tagged "app-*". No production deploy.
- PA-ReleaseMgr (3 members): approve and run production deployments, rotate service-account secrets. Changes require a linked Freshservice change ticket.
- PA-Finance: create and edit invoices in QuickBooks Online. Vendor payment approval goes only to the Controller.
- PA-ITAdmin (2 members): NinjaOne script execution, Defender for Endpoint isolation and live response, Meraki MX firewall edits.
The IT Manager and the Head of Engineering review this matrix twice a year (January and July). Any change needs a Freshservice request approved by the data owner.

Ticket: INC-2291 | Priority: Medium | Opened: 2024-08-06 09:14
Reporter: J. Whitcomb (Project Coordinator)
Summary: User reported an email claiming to be a DocuSign request from a client domain that had one letter changed. The user did not click the link.
Actions: The analyst pulled the message from 4 mailboxes using the Google Workspace investigation tool. The sender domain was blocked in Gmail. A Graylog search over the last 72 hours of Meraki MX URL logs found no hits on the lookalike domain. Defender for Endpoint showed no related alerts on the affected devices.
Resolution: Closed 2024-08-06 11:02. The case will be used as an example in the September security awareness bulletin.

4.2 Approved Flow Paths
CUI may move only through the paths listed in Appendix B (Approved CUI Flow Register). The IT Security Manager maintains the register. Each entry lists the source zone, destination system, protocol, data owner, and approval date.

4.3 Approval Authority
The Facility Security Officer and the IT Security Manager must both approve any new flow path, or any change to an existing one, through a Zendesk change ticket before the firewall team commits it. A flow that is not in the register is denied by default on the PA-440 firewalls.

4.4 Google Workspace
Shared drives labeled "CUI" are limited to the cui-engineering@pellucidanalytics.com group. External sharing on these drives is turned off in the Admin Console under Drive > Sharing settings > "CUI" OU.

Section 5 – Improper Posting Response
5.1 If CUI is found on any publicly accessible system (corvanelogistics.com, the LinkedIn company page, the shipment-tracking portal, or a public cloud share), the person who finds it opens a Freshservice ticket in the "CUI Spill – Public" category. This category is set to Priority P1 by default.

5.3 Within 2 business days, the Operations Director tells the affected customer or prime contractor and asks Google and Bing to remove cached copies.
5.4 Before the ticket can close, the root cause must be recorded and the poster must retake CUI handling training.

--- [ACCT-PRO-004_Account_Disablement_Procedure_v2.3.docx] (excerpt)
4.2 Orphaned and Unassigned Accounts
An account becomes orphaned when its named owner leaves Marlowe Hydraulics, moves to a role that has no need for it, or can no longer be identified, such as a shared login whose sponsor has left or a contractor account with no active SOW. The IT Systems Administrator runs the Okta "Users without Manager / Inactive HR Link" report every Monday. Any account with no matching active record in the BambooHR feed is moved to Suspended within 1 business day. Its Okta app assignments are removed, and the matching AD object is disabled and moved to OU=Disabled,DC=marlowe,DC=local. A Jira Service Management ticket (request type: Account Disable – Orphaned) is opened for each account. After 90 days the account is deleted unless the Information Security Manager approves keeping it for legal hold.

This module covers the warning signs our Security Committee has agreed on for an optics manufacturer that handles controlled lens and coating designs. The list is reviewed each January.

6. Unexplained foreign travel or outside contacts asking about our defense-program optics.

**03.02.01 – Literacy Training and Awareness** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Awareness and Training)

Organizations provide basic and advanced levels of security literacy training to system users (including managers, senior executives, system administrators, and contractors) and measures to test the knowledge level of users. Organizations determine the content of literacy training based on specific organizational requirements, the systems to which personnel have authorized access, and work environments (e.g., telework). The content includes an understanding of the need for security and the actions required of users to maintain security and respond to incidents. The content also addresses the need for operations security and the handling of CUI. Security awareness techniques include displaying posters, offering supplies inscribed with security reminders, generating email advisories or notices from organizational officials, displaying logon screen messages, and conducting awareness events using podcasts, videos, and webinars. Security literacy training is conducted at a frequency consistent with applicable laws, directives, regulations, and policies. Updating literacy training content on a regular basis ensures that the content remains relevant. Events that may precipitate an update to literacy training content include assessment or audit findings, security incidents or breaches, or changes in applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Potential indicators and possible precursors of insider threats include behaviors such as inordinate, long-term job dissatisfaction; attempts to gain access to information that is not required for job performance; unexplained access to financial resources; sexual harassment or bullying of fellow employees; workplace violence; and other serious violations of the policies, procedures, rules, directives, or practices of organizations. Organizations may consider tailoring insider threat awareness topics to roles (e.g., training for managers may be focused on specific changes in the behavior of team members, while training for employees may be focused on more general observations). Social engineering is an attempt to deceive an individual into revealing information or taking an action that can be used to breach, compromise, or otherwise adversely impact a system. Social engineering includes phishing, pretexting, impersonation, baiting, quid pro quo, threadjacking, social media exploitation, and tailgating. Social mining is an attempt to gather information about the organization that may be used to support future attacks. Security literacy training includes how to communicate employee and management concerns regarding potential indicators of insider threat and potential and actual instances of social engineering and data mining through appropriate organizational channels in accordance with established policies and procedures.

How should a company approach implementing AC.L2-3.1.17?

**AC.L2-3.1.17 – Wireless Access Protection** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, 3.1.17)

Use a combination of authentication and encryption methods to protect the access to wireless networks. Authenticating users to a wireless access point can be achieved in multiple ways. The most common authentication and encryption methods used include:

WPA2-PSK (WiFi Protected Access-Pre-shared Key) – This method uses a password or passphrase known by the wireless access point and the client (user device). It is common in small companies that have little turnover because the key must be changed each time an employee leaves in order to prevent the terminated employee from connecting to the network without authorization. WPA2 is typically configured to use Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) encryption.

WPA2 Enterprise – This method may be better for larger companies and enterprise networks because authentication is based on the identity of the individual user or device rather than a shared password or passphrase. It typically requires a Remote Authentication Dial-in User Service (RADIUS) server for authentication and can provide higher security than WPA2-PSK.

Open authentication must not be used because it authenticates any user and lacks security capabilities.

Because the use of cryptography in this requirement is to protect the confidentiality of CUI, the cryptography used must meet the criteria specified in requirement SC.L2-3.13.11. AC.L2-3.1.16, AC.L2-3.1.17, and AC.L2-3.1.18 are complementary requirements in that they all establish control for the connection of mobile devices and wireless devices through the use of authentication, authorization, and encryption mechanisms.

**03.05.07 – Password Management** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Identification and Authentication)

Password-based authentication applies to passwords used in single-factor or multi-factor authentication. Long passwords or passphrases are preferable to shorter passwords. Enforced composition rules provide marginal security benefits while decreasing usability. However, organizations may choose to establish and enforce certain rules for password generation (e.g., minimum character length) under certain circumstances. For example, account recovery can occur when a password is forgotten. Cryptographically protected passwords include salted one-way cryptographic hashes of passwords. The list of commonly used, compromised, or expected passwords includes passwords obtained from previous breach corpuses, dictionary words, and repetitive or sequential characters. The list includes context-specific words, such as the name of the service, username, and derivatives thereof. Changing temporary passwords to permanent passwords immediately after system logon ensures that the necessary strength of the authentication mechanism is implemented at the earliest opportunity and reduces susceptibility to authenticator compromises. Long passwords and passphrases can be used to increase the complexity of passwords.

5.3 Periodic Functionality Review
The IT Systems Administrator will review all in-scope assets every quarter (January, April, July, October). In-scope assets are domain controllers, file servers, MES/SMT line workstations, and the FortiGate 60F perimeter firewall. Each review identifies services, listening ports, protocols, firewall policies, and remote connections that are no longer needed or are insecure. **03.05.11 – Authentication Feedback** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Identification and Authentication)

Authentication feedback does not provide information that would allow unauthorized individuals to compromise authentication mechanisms. For example, for desktop or notebook systems with relatively large monitors, the threat may be significant (commonly referred to as shoulder surfing). For mobile devices with small displays, this threat may be less significant and is balanced against the increased likelihood of input errors due to small keyboards. Therefore, the means of obscuring authenticator feedback is selected accordingly. Obscuring feedback includes displaying asterisks when users type passwords into input devices or displaying feedback for a limited time before fully obscuring it.

4.3 Firewall Rule Baseline

Cisco Meraki MX appliances ship with an implicit "allow any" Layer 3 rule that cannot be removed. New permit rules must reference a change number in the Comment field and identify a business owner. The Network Engineer applying the rule is responsible for confirming placement above the deny entry. Syslog for all rules is forwarded to Microsoft Sentinel.

The IT Administrator keeps the following list of logging failure types. Each one triggers an alert in Microsoft Sentinel:
(a) Data connector stops sending: no Heartbeat or SecurityEvent records from any onboarded host for more than 60 minutes.

Section 5: Containment Actions
5.1 Endpoint isolation. Once the on-call Security Analyst confirms a SentinelOne alert at High or Critical severity, they apply "Disconnect from Network" to the affected Mac or Windows host within 15 minutes. The SentinelOne agent keeps its management channel open so the host can still be investigated remotely.

5.4 Every action is logged as a work note on the ServiceNow Security Incident, with a timestamp and the operator's initials. Containment is not marked complete until the Incident Lead approves the "Contained" state.

4.3 Inventory Maintenance Across the Life Cycle
The IT Operations Lead owns the System Component Inventory (SCI), which is kept in ManageEngine Endpoint Central and linked to Jira Service Management asset records. The SCI is updated at each life cycle gate:
• Initiation/Acquisition: purchase request ticket (ITPROC-) adds a "Planned" record before the item is received.
• Implementation: the Endpoint Central agent and SentinelOne sensor must report in before the record moves to "In Service."
• Operation/Maintenance: Endpoint Central scans hardware and software every 24 hours. Any firmware or OS change rewrites the record automatically.
• Disposal: a Datto SIRIS final backup is confirmed, the drive is wiped, and the record is set to "Retired" and kept for 3 years.
Once a quarter, the Security Engineer compares the SCI against Meraki MX DHCP client lists and Okta device registrations. Any differences are opened as Jira tickets and must be fixed within 10 business days.

4.6 Disabling Accounts No Longer Required
An account is no longer required if the user leaves, transfers to a role that does not need the access, finishes a contract, or the system the account supports is retired. In these cases the following time limits apply:
- Involuntary termination: the JumpCloud user is suspended within 1 hour of HR notice.
- Voluntary separation or contract end: the account is suspended by 23:59 local time on the last working day.
- Role change: access the new role does not need is removed within 2 business days.
- Service accounts tied to a decommissioned asset: the account is disabled within 5 business days of the decommission ticket.
IT Operations owns these actions. The IT Security Lead checks compliance every month. Disabled accounts are kept for 90 days, then deleted. Google Workspace mailboxes go to the manager before the account is deleted.

4.2 Log Integrity Controls
All security logs from Okta, Sophos Central, NinjaOne, and the FortiGate 60F are forwarded to Blumira within 5 minutes of generation. --- [NET-STD-004_Firewall_Rule_Management_Standard_v3.2.docx] (excerpt)
4.1 Default Posture. Every pfSense interface (WAN, LAN, ENG_CUI, MFG_OT, GUEST) ends with an explicit "Block all – default deny" rule at the bottom of its ruleset, and logging is turned on for that rule. Any traffic not matched by an approved pass rule above it is dropped. Outbound traffic from ENG_CUI is held to the same restriction, so there is no implicit allow-all egress.
4.2 Exceptions. A pass rule is added only after an approved Zendesk change request lists the source, destination, port/protocol, business justification, and an expiration or review date. The Network Administrator implements the rule. The IT Security Lead approves it. Each rule description has to include the ticket number (example: "ZD-41877 Veeam proxy to repo TCP 2500-3300").
4.3 Review. Every quarter, IT Security reviews all pass rules. Rules with no traffic hits in 90 days, or with no current ticket, are disabled and then deleted after 30 days.

All network logons to Corvane Logistics domain accounts (CORVANE.LOCAL), whether standard user or administrative, must use Kerberos v5 with AES256 encryption. When Splunk Cloud alerts that a source has stopped forwarding (the "Forwarder Silent > 30 min" search runs every 15 minutes), the IT Administrator must take these steps on top of the standard alert:

4.2 Nonessential Services Definition
For Marlowe Hydraulics, a nonessential service is any program, OS feature, listening port, protocol, or background service that does not appear in the Approved Services Baseline (Appendix B). If a service is missing from the baseline, it counts as nonessential and is disabled by default. Specific examples: Windows Remote Registry, Print Spooler on servers, SMBv1, Telnet client/server, LLMNR, NetBIOS over TCP/IP, Xbox Game services, Windows Fax and Scan, and peer-to-peer file sharing clients. A service may run only if the Security Lead approves a business justification and logs it in Freshservice under the 'Service Exception' category. Exceptions run for no more than 180 days and must be renewed. The IT Manager reviews Appendix B every quarter, and again after any major Windows feature update.

4.2 Identifying Publicly Accessible Components

The IT/Security Lead maintains the Public-Facing Asset Register and reviews it quarterly and whenever a change request introduces a new inbound service. A component is classified as publicly accessible if it (a) has a pfSense WAN NAT or port-forward rule pointing to it, (b) is reachable from the internet without VPN authentication, or (c) is a vendor-hosted service accepting public logins.

During each quarterly review, the Lead exports the pfSense NAT/Port Forward table (Firewall > NAT) and compares every destination against the register. Any destination not listed must be removed or registered within 5 business days. All registered self-hosted public components must reside on the DMZ interface (OPT1, VLAN 30); placement on LAN or DEV is prohibited. 4.6 Session and Connection Timeouts
Ashgrove Research defines the following inactivity periods for network connections tied to communications sessions:

**CM.L2-3.4.3 – System Change Management** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, 3.4.3)

Tracking, reviewing, approving/disapproving, and logging changes is called configuration change control. Configuration change control for organizational systems involves the systematic proposal, justification, implementation, testing, review, and disposition of changes to the systems, including system upgrades and modifications. Configuration change control includes changes to baseline configurations for components and configuration items of systems, changes to configuration settings for information technology products (e.g., operating systems, applications, firewalls, routers, and mobile devices), unscheduled and unauthorized changes, and changes to remediate vulnerabilities.

Processes for managing configuration changes to systems include Configuration Control Boards or Change Advisory Boards that review and approve proposed changes to systems. For new development systems or systems undergoing major upgrades, organizations consider including representatives from development organizations on the Configuration Control Boards or Change Advisory Boards. Audit logs of changes include activities before and after changes are made to organizational systems and the activities required to implement such changes. NIST SP 800-128 provides guidance on configuration change control.

4.2 Internal Transfers and Role Changes
When HR records a change in department, job code, or program assignment in the HRIS, the HR Generalist opens a "Role Change – Access Review" request in Freshservice within 1 business day of the effective date. The receiving manager lists the access the new duties require. The departing manager confirms which existing access should be removed. IT Operations then:

(c) updates PreVeil workspace membership and Intune device-group assignment;
(d) closes the ticket with before/after group exports attached.

**03.03.08 – Protection of Audit Information** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Audit and Accountability)

Audit information includes the information needed to successfully audit system activity, such as audit records, audit log settings, audit reports, and personally identifiable information. Audit logging tools are programs and devices used to conduct audit and logging activities. The protection of audit information focuses on technical protection and limits the ability to access and execute audit logging tools to authorized individuals. The physical protection of audit information is addressed by media and physical protection requirements. Individuals or roles with privileged access to a system and who are also the subject of an audit by that system may affect the reliability of the audit information by inhibiting audit activities or modifying audit records. Requiring privileged access to be further defined between audit-related privileges and other privileges limits the number of users or roles with audit-related privileges.

4.6 Automatic Session Termination
Graywacke Engineering ends user sessions automatically when any of the following occurs:

(e) Microsoft Defender for Endpoint raises a High severity alert, and the device is isolated through automated response.

Section 4.1 – Network Segmentation. Blue Heron Fabrication follows a zoned architecture enforced on the Cisco Meraki MX250 at the Dayton plant. **03.17.01 – Supply Chain Risk Management Plan** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Supply Chain Risk Management)

Dependence on the products, systems, and services of external providers and the nature of the relationships with those providers present an increasing level of risk to an organization. Threat actions that may increase security risks include unauthorized production, the insertion or use of counterfeits, tampering, poor manufacturing and development practices in the supply chain, theft, and the insertion of malicious software, firmware, and hardware. Supply chain risks can be endemic or systemic within a system, component, or service. Managing supply chain risks is a complex, multifaceted undertaking that requires a coordinated effort across an organization to build trust relationships and communicate with internal and external stakeholders. Supply chain risk management (SCRM) activities include identifying and assessing risks, determining appropriate risk response actions, developing SCRM plans to document response actions, and monitoring performance against the plans. The system-level SCRM plan is implementation-specific and provides constraints, policy implementation, requirements, and implications. It can either be stand-alone or incorporated into system security plans. The SCRM plan addresses the management, implementation, and monitoring of SCRM requirements and the development or sustainment of systems across the system development life cycle to support mission and business functions. Because supply chains can differ significantly across and within organizations, SCRM plans are tailored to individual program, organizational, and operational contexts.

Why does MP.L2-3.8.3 matter?

**MP.L2-3.8.3 – Media Disposal** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, 3.8.3)

This requirement applies to all system media, digital and non-digital, subject to disposal or reuse. Examples include: digital media found in workstations, network components, scanners, copiers, printers, notebook computers, and mobile devices; and non-digital media such as paper and microfilm. The sanitization process removes information from the media such that the information cannot be retrieved or reconstructed. Sanitization techniques, including clearing, purging, cryptographic erase, and destruction, prevent the disclosure of information to unauthorized individuals when such media is released for reuse or disposal. Organizations determine the appropriate sanitization methods, recognizing that destruction may be necessary when other methods cannot be applied to the media requiring sanitization. Organizations use discretion on the employment of sanitization techniques and procedures for media containing information that is in the public domain or publicly releasable or deemed to have no adverse impact on organizations or individuals if released for reuse or disposal. Sanitization of non-digital media includes destruction, removing CUI from documents, or redacting selected sections or words from a document by obscuring the redacted sections or words in a manner equivalent in effectiveness to removing the words or sections from the document. NARA policy and guidance control sanitization processes. NIST SP 800-88 provides guidance on media sanitization.

**IA.L2-3.5.2 – Authentication** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, 3.5.2)

Before a person or device is given system access, verify that the user or device is who or what it claims to be. This verification is called authentication. The most common way to verify identity is using a username and a hard-to-guess password.

Some devices ship with default usernames and passwords. Some devices ship with a default username (e.g., admin) and password. A default username and password must be immediately changed to something unique. Default passwords may be well known to the public, easily found in a search, or easy to guess, allowing an unauthorized person to access the system.

4.2 Report Generation from Stored Events
Analysts build audit reports in Graylog with saved searches and dashboards only. Searches run against the indexed message store and never change stored messages. Pipeline rules on the "AD-Security" and "PA440-Traffic" streams may add fields such as site_code and asset_owner. They may not overwrite or drop the original message, source, or timestamp fields. If a report needs records outside Graylog, the IT Systems Administrator exports them as CSV with the original timestamp column left in place. Copies used for spreadsheet sorting or filtering are saved as a separate file named with the suffix _working. The unmodified export stays in \\corv-fs01\Audit\Exports\Originals\ under read-only NTFS permissions. Only members of the GG-Audit-Admins group can write to that folder.

- Medium (4.0–6.9): 60 calendar days

--- [Audit_Logging_Standard_v3.2.docx] (excerpt)
4.3 Time Stamp Format
All systems that generate audit records must write time stamps in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Where a product cannot be set to UTC natively, the record must carry an explicit offset (e.g., 2024-05-14T09:12:44.318-05:00), and Graylog normalizes it to UTC on ingest. Records must have at least millisecond (0.001 s) granularity. Hosts with only one-second precision must be logged as exceptions in the risk register.
Time source: pfSense (fw-core-01) runs the NTP service and syncs to time.nist.gov and 0.us.pool.ntp.org. All other servers and endpoints sync to pfSense. The Infrastructure Lead reviews clock drift monthly. Drift over 1 second opens a Jira Service Management ticket.

**03.04.02 – Configuration Settings** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Configuration Management)

Configuration settings are the set of parameters that can be changed in hardware, software, or firmware components of the system and that affect the security posture or functionality of the system. Security-related configuration settings can be defined for systems (e.g., servers, workstations), input and output devices (e.g., scanners, copiers, printers), network components (e.g., firewalls, routers, gateways, voice and data switches, wireless access points, network appliances, sensors), operating systems, middleware, and applications. Security parameters are those parameters that impact the security state of the system, including the parameters required to satisfy other security requirements. Security parameters include registry settings; account, file, and directory permission settings (i.e., privileges); and settings for functions, ports, protocols, and remote connections. Organizations establish organization-wide configuration settings and subsequently derive specific configuration settings for the system. The established settings become part of the system’s configuration baseline. Common secure configurations (also referred to as security configuration checklists, lockdown and hardening guides, security reference guides, and security technical implementation guides) provide recognized, standardized, and established benchmarks that stipulate secure configuration settings for specific information technology platforms/products and instructions for configuring those system components to meet operational requirements. Common secure configurations can be developed by a variety of organizations, including information technology product developers, manufacturers, vendors, consortia, academia, industry, federal agencies, and other organizations in the public and private sectors.

Section 4.3 – Character Change on Password Reset
When a user creates a new password, at least 4 characters in the new password must differ from the immediately preceding password, regardless of their position. The new password may not contain the user's previous password as a substring, and it may not repeat any of the last 24 passwords. Changing only case or adding or incrementing a trailing digit (e.g., Summer2024! → Summer2025!) does not count as a change and is not allowed. All remote and administrative sessions into the Corvane Logistics environment must be mutually authenticated and protected against hijacking or replay. **03.03.01 – Event Logging** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Audit and Accountability)

An event is any observable occurrence in a system, including unlawful or unauthorized system activity. Organizations identify event types for which a logging functionality is needed. This includes events that are relevant to the security of systems and the environments in which those systems operate to meet specific and ongoing auditing needs. Event types can include password changes, the execution of privileged functions, failed logons or accesses related to systems, administrative privilege usage, or third-party credential usage. In determining event types that require logging, organizations consider the system monitoring and auditing that are appropriate for each of the security requirements. When defining event types, organizations consider the logging necessary to cover related events, such as the steps in distributed, transaction-based processes (e.g., processes that are distributed across multiple organizations) and actions that occur in service-oriented or cloud-based architectures. Monitoring and auditing requirements can be balanced with other system needs. For example, organizations may determine that systems must have the capability to log every file access — both successful and unsuccessful — but only activate that capability under specific circumstances due to the potential burden on system performance. The event types that are logged by organizations may change over time. Reviewing and updating the set of logged event types are necessary to ensure that the current set of event types remains relevant.

**IR.L2-3.6.1 – Incident Handling** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, 3.6.1)

Incident handling capabilities prepare your organization to respond to incidents and may:
- identify people inside and outside your organization you may need to contact during an incident; establish a way to report incidents, such as an email address or a phone number; establish a system for tracking incidents; and determine a place and a way to store evidence of an incident.

Software and hardware may be required to analyze incidents when they occur. Incident prevention activities are also part of an incident-handling capability. The incident-handling team provides input for such things as risk assessments and training. OSAs detect incidents using different indicators. Indicators may include:
- alerts from sensors or antivirus software;
- a filename that looks unusual; and log entries that raise concern.

After detecting an incident, an incident response team performs analysis. This requires some knowledge of normal network operations. The incident should be documented including all the log entries associated with the incident.

Containment of the incident is a critical step to stop the damage the incident is causing to your network. Containment activities should be based on previously defined organizational priorities and assessment of risk. Recovery activities restore systems to pre-incident functionality and address its underlying causes. Organizations should use recovery activities as a means of improving their overall resilience to future attacks.

3. Adopted Principles
We apply the following principles to any new system or change to an existing component (servers, endpoints, firewall rulesets, SaaS integrations):
(a) Least privilege: service accounts in Active Directory are scoped to a single function, and nobody is added to Domain Admins.
(b) Defense in depth: every endpoint runs both Jamf Pro configuration profiles and CrowdStrike Falcon prevention policies. Neither one is relied on alone.
(c) Secure defaults: new PA-440 rules start from deny-all, and each allow rule needs a named owner.
(d) Minimized attack surface: unused services are turned off before deployment.
(e) Fail secure: if authentication or logging fails, access is denied rather than allowed.
The IT & Security Lead reviews each design against this list. The outcome goes on the ServiceNow change record in the "Security Design Review" field. The list is reviewed every year, and the next review is due 2025-03-01.

Ironbark Defense Solutions permits only FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 validated modules to protect CUI confidentiality. Approved types:

4.3 Authenticator Refresh Schedule
Tidewater Systems Group does not require periodic password changes for standard user accounts protected by Microsoft Entra ID phishing-resistant MFA. The following refresh intervals apply instead:
- Privileged admin accounts (Global Admin, Intune Admin, Falcon Console Admin): password changed every 90 days
- Service accounts (Veeam, Wazuh agents, PA-440 API): credentials rotated every 180 days and logged in the Privileged Credential Register
- Shared break-glass accounts: changed after each use, and at least every 12 months

The company treats the following as audit logging failures requiring an alert: (a) loss of log transmission from any in-scope source to Splunk Cloud beyond the thresholds in the Audit Log Failure Alert Catalog; (b) deliberate or accidental clearing of local audit logs; (c) local log storage reaching capacity; (d) ingestion delays of cloud audit sources, including Entra ID and Microsoft 365 GCC unified audit log; and (e) Defender for Endpoint sensors reporting an unhealthy state. 4.2 Session Establishment. Any administrator or approved vendor technician who performs maintenance or diagnostics from outside the Ostrander Machine Works facility has to connect through the FortiGate 60F SSL-VPN (portal "omw-maint"). Before a tunnel is established, the user authenticates with SAML 2.0 to Okta. 4.3 Event-Driven Application Scans
When a new CVE or vendor advisory affects an application in the Fennwick Application Inventory (FWM-INV-002), the IT Security Lead opens a Zendesk ticket tagged "vuln-trigger" within 1 business day of the advisory being published. **03.08.01 – Media Storage** (NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, Media Protection)

System media include digital and non-digital media. Digital media include diskettes, flash drives, magnetic tapes, external or removable solid state or magnetic drives, compact discs, and digital versatile discs. Non-digital media include paper and microfilm. Physically controlling stored media includes conducting inventories, establishing procedures to allow individuals to check out and return media to libraries, and maintaining accountability for stored media. Secure storage includes a locked drawer, desk, or cabinet or a controlled media library. Controlled areas provide physical and procedural controls to meet the requirements established for protecting information and systems. Sanitization techniques (e.g., destroying, cryptographically erasing, clearing, and purging) prevent the disclosure of CUI to unauthorized individuals. The sanitization process removes CUI from media such that the information cannot be retrieved or reconstructed.

4.2 Detection of Unapproved Connections
The Security Operations Analyst monitors inbound and outbound connections at all three sites (Rochester plant, Tucson coating facility, HQ) using Cisco Meraki MX security appliances. Meraki syslog (flows, IDS/IPS, URL events) forwards to Splunk Cloud index net_meraki. Defender for Endpoint network events forward to index edr_mde.
The following conditions generate an alert in Splunk and auto-create a Jira Service Management ticket in the SECOPS project:
- Outbound traffic to any destination on the Meraki Group Policy deny list or to countries outside the geo-allow list
- Any client MAC not registered in Intune or the Meraki Systems Manager inventory connecting to the CORP or MFG VLANs
- RDP, SSH, or SMB sessions from the guest VLAN (VLAN 40) toward internal subnets
P2 tickets must be triaged within 4 business hours.

4.2 Defining Essential Services
Each system class (corporate endpoint, engineering workstation, production line controller, server) has a written baseline. Baselines are reviewed every year, and also within 30 days of any major platform change, such as a new Jamf Pro configuration profile set or a firmware upgrade on the PA-440 firewalls. If a baseline is not reviewed within 13 months, it is flagged on the quarterly GRC dashboard.

4.4 Additions
To add a service, submit a Zendesk request with the category "Service Exception". The request must state the port or protocol, the scope, the duration, and the compensating controls.

Removable media holding CUI (USB drives, external SSDs, optical discs) must be encrypted before any CUI is written to it.
